```{r setup}
library(fnware)
```

## Returning a default

`fallback()` catches a failure and returns a default instead of signalling it.

```{r value}
safe_sqrt := fallback(value = NA_real_) %@% function(x) {
  if (x < 0) stop("negative") else sqrt(x)
}
safe_sqrt(4)
safe_sqrt(-1)
```

To compute the result from the failure, pass a `handler`. It receives the
condition:

```{r handler}
describe := fallback(handler = function(cnd) conditionMessage(cnd)) %@%
  function() stop("boom")
describe()
```

Only errors are caught by default. Set `class` to catch other conditions, such
as `class = "warning"`. A caught condition ends the call, as with `tryCatch()`.

## Stacking with retry and the circuit breaker

Put `fallback()` outermost. The default is then used only once `retry()` has
given up, or once `circuit_breaker()` has opened:

```{r stack}
calls <- 0
fetch := fallback(value = "cached") %@%
  circuit_breaker(failures = 3) %@%
  retry(stop = stop_after_attempt(2)) %@%
  function(url) {
    calls <<- calls + 1
    stop("down")
  }

fetch("x")
calls
```

## Promises

`async_fallback()` does the same for functions that return a promise. The
promise resolves to the default if the function rejects with a matching
condition, and other rejections carry on unchanged. It needs the promises
package.

```{r async, eval = FALSE}
f := async_fallback(value = "default") %@% function() stop("boom")
promises::then(f(), print)
```

## Running once

`once()` runs a function on its first successful call and returns that result
every time after, ignoring later arguments. It suits setup that should happen a
single time.

```{r once}
setup := once %@% function() {
  cat("setting up\n")
  42
}
setup()
setup()
```

An error stores nothing, so the next call tries again. Unlike `cache()`, which
keeps a result per set of arguments, `once()` keeps one result whatever the
arguments.
